scenes.headline: Beyond the qubit count

deck.text: How to judge whether a quantum computing announcement shows real progress

narration: A processor with a thousand qubits makes a good headline.
But the qubit count tells you how big a machine is, not what it can do.
Here are six questions that separate real progress from a large number, applied to two recent results.

scenes.heading: Errors compound
scenes.source: Our calculation of (1 − p)ᴺ for independent errors

notes.text: 1 in 100: a hundred steps run cleanly 37% of the time
1 in 1,000: ten thousand steps, once in 22,000 tries
1 in a million: the same steps, 99% of the time
Useful algorithms: millions to billions of operations

narration: Every operation on today's quantum hardware has some chance of failing, and a computation is a long chain of operations.
If each operation fails with probability p, all N of them succeed with probability about one minus p, to the power N.
At one error in a hundred, the chance of a clean run collapses after about a hundred operations.
At one in a thousand, ten thousand steps run cleanly only about once in twenty-two thousand attempts.
At one error in a million, the same ten thousand steps succeed ninety-nine percent of the time.
Useful algorithms need millions to billions of operations, so adding qubits at a high error rate does not help: it gives errors more places to happen.

scenes.heading: How low must errors go?

stats.label: error rate for the simplest useful applications
the best physical error rates today

narration: How low does the error rate need to go?
Microsoft's quantum team, writing with John Martinis in September 2026, puts it at about one in ten billion for the simplest useful applications.
For the most demanding, it is about one in a million billion.
No physical qubit comes close.
So the real question behind a headline is how close a machine gets to reliable operation, and at what cost.

scenes.heading: What exactly is being counted?

items.text: Physical qubit: one device, such as an ion, an atom or a circuit
Logical qubit: information spread over many, by a code
Surface code of distance \(d\): about \(2d^2\) physical qubits
Corrected over many rounds, or detected once and discarded?
Better than its parts? Google 2024: distance 7 lasted 2.4× longer

narration: The first question is what exactly is being counted.
A physical qubit is one device: an ion, an atom or a superconducting circuit.
A logical qubit spreads information over many physical qubits with an error-correcting code, so that errors can be found and undone.
A surface code of distance d uses about two d squared physical qubits.
Check whether errors were corrected over many rounds, or only detected once, with the failed runs thrown away.
And check whether the logical qubit beats its own parts: in Google's 2024 experiment, the distance-seven logical memory outlived the best physical qubit by a factor of about 2.4.

scenes.heading: How good is each operation?

items.text: Median two-qubit error across the device, not the best pair
An average (randomized benchmarking) or the worst case?
Measurement, idling, leakage and crosstalk included?
Operations that fit in the coherence time, not coherence alone

narration: Second: how good is each operation?
Two-qubit gates are usually the weakest link, and a headline fidelity is often the best pair on the chip, so ask for the median across the whole device.
Ask how the figure was measured.
Randomized benchmarking reports an average, and small systematic over-rotations can look tiny on average yet add up over a long circuit.
Measurement errors, idling errors, leakage and crosstalk count too.
And long coherence times mean little on their own: what counts is how many operations fit inside them.

scenes.heading: Does the error fall as the code grows?
scenes.source: Google Quantum AI, Nature 638 (2025); Lavasani et al., arXiv:2610.24077; extrapolation ours

notes.text: Billionfold: d ≈ 59, about 7,000 qubits, against d ≈ 21, about 900

narration: Third, and most informative: does the logical error fall as the code grows?
Error correction only helps below a threshold; above it, a bigger code just collects more errors.
The key number is the suppression factor, Λ: how much the logical error falls each time the distance grows by two.
Google's 2024 surface-code experiment measured about 2.1, across distances three, five and seven.
Quantinuum's 2026 colour-code preprint reports about twelve.
The two count errors differently, so compare their slopes, not their absolute values.
If each trend continued, a billionfold reduction would need distance about 59 at the first rate, but about 21 at the second.
That is roughly seven thousand physical qubits per logical qubit, against nine hundred.
This is our extrapolation, and rare correlated errors, from cosmic rays or leakage, are what could break it.

scenes.heading: Could a classical computer do the same?
scenes.source: Arute et al., Nature 574 (2019); IBM Research (2019); Pan, Chen and Zhang, PRL 129 (2022)
columns: Classical cost of Google's 53-qubit sampling task

cells: About 10,000 years on a supercomputer (200 s on the processor)
About 2.5 days for an ideal classical simulation
About 15 hours on 512 GPUs, at the experiment's fidelity

narration: Fourth: could a classical computer do the same?
Many beyond-classical demonstrations run tasks chosen because they are hard to simulate, and their classical cost is a moving target.
In 2019, Google estimated that its fifty-three-qubit sampling task, finished in two hundred seconds, would take a supercomputer about ten thousand years.
IBM answered that an ideal classical simulation would take about two and a half days.
By 2022, Pan, Chen and Zhang had done it in about fifteen hours on 512 GPUs, at the experiment's low fidelity.
So ask whether the comparison used the best known classical method, and whether the output can be checked at all.

footer.text: Ask: was it the best known classical method, and can the output be checked?

scenes.heading: What would a useful task need?
scenes.source: Gidney, arXiv:2505.15917 (2025); Pappalardo et al., arXiv:2610.37839 (preprint)

cells: bit flips rarer than once a century; seconds measured today

narration: Fifth: what would a useful task actually need?
A resource estimate turns an algorithm into hardware, and its headline number always rests on assumptions.
Craig Gidney's 2025 estimate for breaking 2048-bit RSA needs fewer than a million noisy qubits for under a week, assuming a one-in-a-thousand gate error and a one-microsecond correction cycle.
A 2026 Alice and Bob preprint needs only 22,593 cat qubits, but assumes bit flips rarer than once a century per qubit, where seconds are measured today.
Lower qubit counts usually rest on stronger assumptions, so compare the assumptions, not the counts.

footer.text: Compare the assumptions, not the qubit counts

scenes.heading: Speed matters as much as size

text.text: Correction cycles a thousand times slower turn a one-week computation into one of about two decades.

sub.text: A nearer milestone (Preskill): machines that run about a million operations reliably, “megaquop” machines

scenes.source: J. Preskill, Beyond NISQ: The Megaquop Machine, arXiv:2502.17368 (2025)
narration: Speed matters as much as size.
On hardware whose correction cycles are a thousand times slower, a one-week computation becomes one of about two decades.
John Preskill has proposed a nearer milestone: error-corrected machines running about a million operations reliably, which he calls megaquop machines.

scenes.heading: Result, plan or product?
scenes.source: US Department of War, Quantum Benchmarking Initiative release (October 2026)

cells: Referees checked the method and the claims
The authors' account, not yet reviewed
What users can run today, with published limits

narration: Sixth: is it a result, a plan or a product?
Announcements mix statements of very different weight, and the wording rarely says which is which.
A peer-reviewed paper means referees checked the method.
A preprint is the authors' account, not yet reviewed.
An independent replication means another group reproduced the result.
A roadmap is an intended machine and date.
Funding is money committed, not capability.
And a cloud product is what users can run today.
Programmes that fund the field increasingly pay for verified performance: DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative verifies hardware in its final stage.

footer.text: DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative verifies hardware in its final stage

scenes.heading: Two real announcements, scored
scenes.source: Quantinuum release, 19 October 2026; arXiv:2610.24077; The Quantum Insider, 31 July 2026

cells: One logical qubit; colour codes of distance 3 to 7
About 12 times less error per distance step
Sampling task said to exceed leading classical methods

cells.text: Preprint; the 2029 machine is a goal
arXiv paper; review status not stated

narration: Here are the questions applied to two recent results.
Quantinuum's October 2026 result counts one logical qubit, on colour codes of distance three to seven, with about twelve times less error per distance step.
It is a memory, not a computation, and it is a preprint; its 2029 machine is a goal.
IBM and the University of Chicago, in July 2026, reported seventy logical qubits running a sampling task said to exceed leading classical methods, with a statistical lower bound on fidelity.
That is not a code-size scaling experiment, and the coverage does not state its review status.
Neither answers every question, and neither claims to.
A headline about a thousand-qubit processor, by contrast, answers only one: how big the machine is.

footer.text: Neither answers every question. A 1,000-qubit headline answers only one: how big?

scenes.heading: The checklist

cells: Logical qubits, with the code and distance stated
Median two-qubit error across the device
Error falling across three or more code sizes
The best known method, and a verifiable output

narration: To sum up, here is the checklist.
Look for logical qubits with the code and distance stated, and the median two-qubit error across the device.
Look for error falling across three or more code sizes, measured over repeated rounds with decoding in time.
Look for comparisons against the best known classical method, and resource estimates whose assumptions are close to measured values.
And look for peer review or independent replication, rather than roadmap dates and funding reported as results.
Few announcements answer all six questions, and that is normal.
The point is to know which ones a result answers, and which it leaves open.

footer.text: Know which questions a result answers, and which it leaves open
